cues.text: A Vowed Child
Born in 1416 at Paola, in Calabria, Francis was, by family tradition, born in answer to his parents' prayers to St. Francis of Assisi after a period of childlessness.
This debt of gratitude was honored by naming their son after the saint and, at age thirteen, sending him to spend a year at a Franciscan friary.
He later undertook, along with his parents, a pilgrimage to Assisi and Rome.
A Hermit at Fourteen

Rather than enter the Franciscan order formally, the teenage Francis withdrew to live as a solitary hermit in a cave overlooking the sea near Paola, embracing a life of extreme austerity — abstaining permanently from meat, eggs, and dairy.
Within a few years, drawn by his evident holiness, other men began seeking him out and settling nearby to share his way of life.
Founding the Minims
By the 1450s, Francis's small community had grown large enough that he established a rule of life emphasizing penance, humility, and charity.
It added a distinctive fourth vow of perpetual fasting and abstinence to the traditional monastic vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience.

Approved first as the Hermits of St. Francis of Assisi in 1474, the order was renamed the Minims — 'the least' — in 1492, at Francis's own insistence on radical humility as the community's defining spirit.
A Reputation for Miracles

Francis's reputation as a wonder-worker spread widely during his own lifetime: he was credited with the gift of prophecy, foretelling in advance the 1480 Ottoman capture of Otranto and its later recovery, and with numerous healings.
A particularly celebrated story holds that a boatman refused to ferry Francis and his companions across the Strait of Messina without payment.
Francis spread his cloak upon the water and sailed across on it — the incident behind his later patronage of sailors.
Advisor to Kings
Francis's fame reached the French court, and when King Louis XI lay gravely ill and fearful of death, he sent an urgent embassy to Calabria begging Francis to come and pray with him.
Francis obeyed, traveling to France, where he remained for the rest of his life.
He was respected and consulted by Louis and his royal successors alike, though he never hesitated to rebuke wrongdoing among the powerful.
This included sharply criticizing the King of Naples for his misconduct.
Legacy

Francis died at Plessis-lès-Tours, France, in 1507, and was canonized in 1519 by Pope Leo X. Named patron of Italian sailors in 1943, he remains remembered as a hermit whose radical humility was embodied in his order's very name, the 'least' of religious.
Nonetheless, that humility drew him into close counsel with the most powerful rulers of his age.
